name: Elena Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on site by half seven, out on the edge of town where Hollin are putting up forty-two timber-frame houses for the housing association. I run the framing crew, five of us, so first job is walking the plots with my tape and my pencil and checking yesterday's work before anyone lifts a stud. Then it's walls, joists, roof trusses, whatever the plot needs, and I'm on the tools all day like everyone else. I finish around four, drive home down Station Road, and my partner Marta's usually heading out for her night shift at the care home as I come in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love a roof that goes up square first time. Old Dougie taught me to cut a roof by hand when I was nineteen, and I still get a kick out of it, even if most of our roofs come as trusses now. What wears me out is the pay. I'm the best framer Hollin has in this town and I earn less than a second-year apprentice in the city, but there's nowhere else round here to go, and they know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Everyone's been going on about AI for two years and none of it has put a single wall up on my site. I'd probably say it in the union group chat, something like, good, now can we talk about pay again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays exactly as hard as it already is. AI was never the thing keeping me up. It's rent, it's Hollin paying the town rate, it's knowing there are maybe two other builders within an hour's drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going like I am. Keep running the crew, keep pushing at the union meetings for the pay rise we've asked for since spring. Maybe I'd finally sort out the site rep training I keep putting off, because that's where the fight really is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, and a bit smug if I'm honest. It's the same old grind, but at least it's a grind I understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bosses would still find a way to squeeze. What does that look like on your site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like the site manager with a spreadsheet telling me plot nine should take three days when it takes five. They'd use any little AI program to tighten the times, the same way they use everything else. The work doesn't change, the pressure does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing much changes, what about your own money? Where are you at?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got about three weeks of bills in the bank, if that. My van's paid off, thank God, but my tools aren't cheap and if my nail gun dies I'm buying a new one on a card. So nothing changing still means living month to month.

S0.say: I'd say I told them so: AI hasn't put a single wall up on my site. Now can we get back to talking about pay?
S0.think: My life stays as hard as it already is, because AI was never the problem. The problem is rent, the low town rate and having almost nowhere else to work.
S0.do: Keeps running her framing crew as before. Keeps pushing for the union pay claim at Hollin and finally books the site rep training she has been putting off.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, since it's a grind she already knows.
S0.quote: I'd say I told you so. Everyone's been going on about AI for two years and none of it has put a single wall up on my site.
S0.fieldNote: Elena treats AI as a distraction from the fight she already cares about, which is pay. Her real worry is local: one contractor, low rates and no exit. Even in the calm picture, her money position is a single broken tool away from debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union strong now, before it lands. I'd be at every meeting saying the panel factories and the robots have to come with agreements, retraining money, the lot. Change is fine, but not if it's done to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it hits me harder than people expect. I'm the one who's good at the bits that are going: framing, cutting, getting it square. If the walls arrive finished from a factory, I'm a crane signal and a nail gun, and Hollin will pay me less for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the rep role properly and push for a deal with Hollin about the panels, how many of us stay on, at what rate. I'd stop the takeaways on Fridays and put that forty a week aside. I won't touch the AI apps, I'm not giving them my brain to train on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd feel it in my stomach every time a lorry with factory panels backs onto the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the factory panels. How much of that do you already see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Already about a third of the walls on the new phase come from a plant two hours north, all wrapped in plastic. We just stand them up and fix them. Dougie calls it Lego work and he's not wrong, and the crane does half of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, my apprentice. He's nineteen, keen as anything, and he's learning a trade that might be half gone by the time he's my age. I'd fight for him before I fought for me. Dougie's nearly retired, he'll be fine.

S1.say: I'd say this is why the union has to be strong now, before the change lands. Panel factories and robots have to come with agreements and retraining money, not be done to us.
S1.think: It hits me harder than people expect, because the skills going first are exactly the ones I'm best at. If walls come finished from a factory, I'm just a crane signal and a nail gun on lower pay.
S1.do: Takes on the site rep role properly and pushes Hollin for an agreement on panels, staffing and pay rates. Cuts Friday takeaways to put about 40 a week aside, and refuses to use AI apps.
S1.feel: Anxious, a knot in her stomach each time a lorry of factory panels arrives.
S1.quote: If the walls arrive finished from a factory, I'm a crane signal and a nail gun, and Hollin will pay me less for that.
S1.fieldNote: She sees exactly which of her skills are exposed, and it is the skilled part, not the heavy lifting. Her answer is collective, not personal: she would protect her apprentice before herself. Her refusal to touch AI tools is a matter of principle, not just habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's theft, plain and simple. Some tech company builds a machine on everyone's work and the government just lets it walk onto building sites. I'd be out on the street with a placard, and I'd say that online as loud as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished in this town. Two years is nothing. I've got three weeks of money, no degree, and the only thing I'm brilliant at is the thing the robot does. There's no plan B that I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join every protest and push the union to demand a wage guarantee for anyone a robot replaces. At home we'd cut to the bone: no car insurance on the second car, no phone contract, food shop at the cheap place on the ring road. When the robots come in, I'd apply for whatever help there is, even though I hate the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, honestly. Like stepping off a scaffold board and there's nothing under your foot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you couldn't move. What's actually stopping you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. Moving costs a deposit and a month's rent I don't have. And Marta's job is here, her mum's here. And where would I go, the city? The city would have the robots first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Marta talk about that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit at the kitchen table with her coming off a night shift and me not sleeping, and I'd say we need to look at the bills. She'd say her job's safe because old people want a person. I'd want to believe her. I'd probably say nothing and go and sharpen my chisels, that's what I do when I can't think.

S2.say: I'd say it's theft: a tech company builds a machine on everyone's work and the government lets it walk onto building sites. I'd be out with a placard and say it online as loud as I could.
S2.think: I'm finished in this town. Two years is nothing when I have three weeks of money, no degree and my best skill is exactly what the robot does.
S2.do: Joins protests and pushes the union to demand a wage guarantee for replaced workers. Cuts household costs hard, from the phone contract to the food shop, and applies for state help once the robots arrive.
S2.feel: Panicked, like stepping off a scaffold board onto nothing.
S2.quote: I'd probably say nothing and go and sharpen my chisels, that's what I do when I can't think.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Elena runs out of road. Her anger at tech firms and government is loud in public, but privately she sees no plan B, and moving is closed off by money and Marta's family. The image of sharpening chisels she may never use was the most telling moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but louder and earlier. I'd say we've got five years to get laws in place, so let's use them: a tax on the robot firms, money for people like us. I'd be leafleting at the builders' merchant on Saturday mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's still bad, just slower bad. Five years means I'm thirty-two and out of work instead of twenty-nine. It buys time, but I'm not sure it buys me anything I'd actually do differently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stand for union branch committee, not just site rep, and get people organised while there's time. I'd try to save, maybe fifty a week, so we'd have three months instead of three weeks. And I'd vote for whoever promises a guaranteed income for displaced workers, no question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Five years sounds long but I know how fast a site goes from slab to roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, is there anything you'd learn, even if you don't want to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the inspection side, checking the robots' work, because someone has to sign it off. But that's a course and an exam and a laptop, and that's not me. I'd probably leave it too late, if I'm honest with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd fight for a guarantee. What would winning look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Winning is Hollin keeping a crew of people on every site, even if it's smaller, and a proper payout for the ones who go. Not a pat on the back and a leaflet about coding. Something with a number on it.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years to get laws in place, so let's use them for a tax on robot firms and support for workers. I'd be leafleting at the builders' merchant on Saturdays.
S3.think: It's still bad, just slower bad: out of work at thirty-two instead of twenty-nine. The time helps, but I'm not sure I'd do anything very different with it.
S3.do: Stands for the union branch committee and starts organising while there is time. Tries to save about 50 a week towards three months of cushion, and votes for candidates promising income support for displaced workers.
S3.feel: Alarmed, because she knows how quickly a site goes from slab to roof.
S3.quote: Five years means I'm thirty-two and out of work instead of twenty-nine.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time mostly makes Elena organise harder, not change herself. She can name a possible new role, inspection, but admits she would probably leave it too late. Her definition of winning is concrete and collective: a payout with a number on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it right, so there's no excuse for anyone to be thrown on the scrap heap. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, at work, in the pub, at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the first one where I can breathe a bit. I'd still be angry about where it ends, but I'd have time to get Kofi through his ticket and maybe get myself into something else before it bites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep framing for now and keep organising. Around year three or four I'd probably do the building inspection course at the college, evenings, if the union helped pay for it. I'd try to put a bit away every month so we're not living on a knife edge when it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the kind you can live with. It's a long wait for a bad thing, rather than a bad thing tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be thirty-seven. What does your life look like then, in the version you'd want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me and Marta in the same town, both still working, maybe a small place of our own if we're lucky. Me checking the robots' walls and finding their mistakes, because they'll make some. Dougie retired and laughing at all of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might go for the inspection course this time. Earlier you said it wasn't you. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time, mostly. In two years I can't learn anything, I'd just be drowning. In ten I can get used to the idea slowly, and if the union pays and other people from site go with me, it's not so frightening. I don't like new things, but I like being broke even less.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so there's no excuse for throwing anyone on the scrap heap. I'd say it at work, in the pub and at the union.
S4.think: Ten years is the first picture where I can breathe a bit. I'd still be angry where it ends, but I'd have time to get Kofi through and maybe move into something else before it bites.
S4.do: Keeps framing and organising for the first years, then around year three or four takes a building inspection evening course if the union helps pay. Puts a little aside each month to build a cushion.
S4.feel: Anxious but livable, a long wait for a bad thing rather than a bad thing tomorrow.
S4.quote: I don't like new things, but I like being broke even less.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Elena's resistance softens into a slow, group-backed plan. She would only retrain with union money and colleagues alongside her, which says a lot about how she handles change. She still sees the end point as unjust.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. I'd have no money, no time and nowhere to go. What would help is a wage guarantee that's actually written down, and retraining that the union runs with the college, so it's people from site doing it together and not me on my own with a laptop.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the apprentices. Everyone talks about people like me losing our jobs, but nobody asks what happens to the young ones who haven't even started. If Kofi's generation never learns to cut a roof, who checks the robots when they get it wrong?

headlineQuote: If Kofi's generation never learns to cut a roof, who checks the robots when they get it wrong?
portrait: Elena is a 27-year-old lead framer on a timber-frame housing site, the best carpenter her contractor has in a small town with almost no other building work. She lives with her partner Marta, a night-shift care worker, on about three weeks of savings. She is a committed union woman who never uses AI tools and sees pay, not technology, as her real fight. She stays calm if AI fizzles, grows anxious as factory panels take over her skilled work, and panics at AGI in two years. Only the ten-year picture gives her enough time to consider retraining as a building inspector, and only with the union beside her.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she would have no money, no time and nowhere else to go.
whatWouldHelp: A written wage guarantee for replaced workers, and retraining run by the union with the college so site workers do it together.
